splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing for more current data to inform withdrawal liability calculations.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the supervised release period does not run while the person is a fugitive from supervision.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to create such a common-law doctrine extending punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prevents relitigating any previously presented claim — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than § 2255(h) alone imposes.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, meaning they cannot relitigate any claim previously raised in addition to satisfying § 2255(h) requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution affects whether candidates can challenge mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices before an election takes place.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge state election laws that allegedly dilute or affect the validity of votes, such as extended ballot-receipt deadlines.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not automatically have standing to challenge election procedures and must demonstrate a concrete and particularized injury beyond a generalized interest in lawful elections.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bognet v. Secretary of Commonwealth of Pennsylvania

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) when construing ambiguous provisions in criminal sentencing contexts, such as the Sentencing Guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity trumps deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in criminal cases. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while the Third Circuit has held that agency deference trumps lenity. This split affects how ambiguous criminal sentencing enhancements are resolved.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor deference when interpreting ambiguous provisions in criminal sentencing contexts, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated interpretive power.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that Auer/Kisor deference to agency or Sentencing Commission commentary interpretations takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant readings of ambiguous Guidelines provisions when the commentary reasonably interprets them.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits hold that defendants are disqualified only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits hold that possessing any single criterion is disqualifying. This split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes depending on jurisdiction.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any single criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is disqualifying from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2) can authoritatively expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text itself does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation deserving Stinson deference or impermissibly expands the guideline text. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy drug convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the ambiguous guideline text under Stinson/Kisor and validly includes conspiracy and other inchoate offenses within the definition of 'controlled substance offense.'

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary cannot expand the definition beyond what the text provides, particularly after Kisor's requirement to exhaust traditional tools of construction.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not listed on the federal schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be controlled under federal law, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling. This affects sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that USSG § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include 'an offense under state law' with no textual basis to require the substance to also be federally controlled.

positions.label: State offense must involve a federally controlled substance
positions.summary: Holds that a state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance is also controlled under federal law, applying the categorical approach.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant at a supervised release revocation hearing for the conduct that violated the conditions of supervised release, or whether revocation sentencing must be limited to the breach of trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for the underlying violation conduct at revocation, while other circuits limit the revocation sentence to addressing the breach of the court's trust. This split affects hundreds of supervised release revocations annually and can result in significantly different sentences.

positions.label: Courts may punish for violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly consider and punish the underlying conduct that violated supervised release conditions, not just the breach of judicial trust.

positions.label: Revocation sentencing limited to breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of supervised release revocation is to sanction the breach of the court's trust, not to punish the defendant for the underlying violation conduct, which is separately prosecutable.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (USSG § 1B1.13(b)(6)) permitting such consideration exceeds the Commission's statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law, particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory consecutive 25-year sentences for stacked § 924(c) convictions, can support compassionate release. Some circuits hold the Commission has authority to designate this as an extraordinary and compelling reason, while others hold this exceeds the Commission's power because Congress chose not to make the change retroactive.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes in law cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, including the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction, and the Commission's policy statement to the contrary exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes in law may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release, particularly where the Sentencing Commission's policy statement authorizes such consideration.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to fact or duration of confinement) exclusively through habeas corpus, or whether they may also use civil rights or Bivens actions.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for challenges that go beyond the fact or duration of confinement to encompass terms and conditions, particularly BOP decisions about programming, transfers, and credit calculations under the First Step Act. The Supreme Court has acknowledged but not resolved this question since Preiser v. Rodriguez (1973).

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-affecting claims
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's claim effectively challenges the duration of confinement, including BOP decisions about earned time credits and release dates, habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may challenge conditions of confinement and certain BOP decisions through civil rights actions (§ 1983 or Bivens), even when those decisions affect release timing, because habeas exclusivity applies only to challenges to the core fact or duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appellate deadline applies to appeals from orders on Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether the time limit for appealing a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order follows the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, but at least one circuit applies the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that the 30-day civil appellate deadline applies to Hyde Amendment attorney's fees orders because such motions are civil matters ancillary to the criminal case.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that the 14-day criminal appellate deadline applies because the Hyde Amendment motion arises within and is part of the criminal case.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's assets belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between a Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor. The Ninth Circuit holds that such appreciation inures to the estate, while other courts have held that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects the debtor's interest in post-petition appreciation to encourage good-faith Chapter 13 filings.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with the broad scope of § 541(a), means that post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by limiting the converted estate to property as valued at the original filing date, so post-petition appreciation belongs to the debtor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that orders denying motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Other circuits have taken different approaches to the collateral order doctrine's application to sealing orders, with the First Circuit recognizing appealability in some privacy contexts.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated by post-judgment appeal.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying sealing motions are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because the privacy interest can be vindicated through other means, including expedited appeal after final judgment.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: In re City of New York

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: Circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business and hospitality contexts. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach, suggesting a circuit split on liability standards, available remedies, and the scope of protections for customers in service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for discrimination claims in hospitality or business establishments, potentially allowing claims based on a wider range of conduct.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a narrower standard requiring a more specific showing of discriminatory conduct before liability attaches in hospitality or business settings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
